Consumer protection law obligations: an overview

This chapter sets out the CMA’s views on some of the most important consumer protection law requirements which apply to providers of unregulated legal services. These include businesses’ obligations to ensure that:

prospective consumers have the information they need to make informed decisions[footnote 8]

terms and conditions are fair[footnote 9]

services are performed with reasonable care and skill[footnote 10]

sales practices are not misleading, aggressive or generally unfair[footnote 11]

Discussion of how these obligations may apply in practice to providers of wills, online divorce, and pre-paid probate services follows.

Ensuring that consumers have the information they need to make informed decisions

Businesses must provide prospective consumers with the information they need to make an informed decision. The information provided must be accurate and not misleading.

Misleading actions and omissions

A business breaks consumer law if it fails to give consumers the information they need to make an informed decision. This is known as a misleading omission.[footnote 12] What information is required sometimes depends on the context, and whether omitting it is likely to affect consumers’ decision making, but consumer legislation also specifies information that must always be given. For example, it is unlawful to omit certain listed information from an ‘invitation to purchase.[footnote 13]

A business also breaks the law if it misleads consumers by giving them information which is false or deceptive, where this is likely to affect consumers’ decision making. This is a misleading action.[footnote 14]

Avoiding misleading consumers by omission: what information needs to be provided?

Material information

Where a business informs consumers about any service they are providing, and its price, this is normally an ‘invitation to purchase. Consumer protection law specifies certain information that the business must provide to consumers in this situation, unless the information is already apparent from the context, regardless of whether that is likely to affect consumers’ decisions.[footnote 15]

This material information includes:

a description of the main characteristics of the services that will be provided, including how the services will be delivered and the timing for delivery. This is likely to require clarifying the details of any services which (contrary to a consumer’s reasonable expectations) are not included within the advertised price

the total price of the service, payable by the consumer (including taxes or payments to third-parties) or, where the total price cannot be reasonably calculated in advance, because of the nature of the service, the way the total price will be calculated (enabling the consumer to calculate the total price)

information about the business, such as their identity and business address

if services are to be provided by a third party, details of the business that will provide them

applicable cancellation rights

any arrangements for payment, delivery, performance or complaint handling which depart from the trader’s otherwise published practice

information required to be given to consumers under other legislation

In addition, wherever consumers need information to make an informed decision about the service, what constitutes ‘material information’ is likely to vary depending on the specific legal services being offered and the way those services are presented to consumers. When determining whether consumers have been, or are likely to be, misled by a business’s failure to provide information, the circumstances of the omission would be taken into account.

When assessing whether particular information is ‘material’ businesses should ask: is this information that the average consumer would need to make an informed decision about whether to buy the service? If the answer is ‘yes’, the information should be provided.

The material information should be provided to consumers in a clear, intelligible, unambiguous, and timely way, before they make decisions.

In the context of unregulated will writing, online divorce, and pre-paid probate services generally, businesses are more likely to comply with the law if they provide the following information to consumers (in addition to the information required to be provided with an invitation to purchase):

an explanation of whether the business is regulated by an approved legal services regulator, and whether it is a member of any self-regulatory bodies

details of the level of experience and/or qualifications of the staff involved in delivering the relevant services: this may include, for example, formal qualifications, experience, membership of a regulatory or self-regulatory body, or professional training completed

details of the business’s complaints handling procedure and what (if any) other routes of redress are available to consumers

an explanation of whether or not the business holds professional indemnity insurance

any terms that the consumer might find particularly surprising, or that are otherwise important

Pre-contract information

The law also requires businesses to provide certain pre-contract information in a clear and comprehensible manner.[footnote 16] There is a considerable overlap between information that is likely to be material information and the pre-contract information that must be given to consumers.

The necessary pre-contract information that must be provided includes:[footnote 17]

the main characteristics of the service

The DMCC Act will, once the relevant provisions come into force, introduce new obligations for businesses offering services on a subscription basis. These provisions are expected to come into force no earlier than Autumn 2026.

These include:

a duty to provide or make available certain key pre-contract information,[footnote 60] including specific requirements where the contract is entered into online[footnote 61]

giving consumers regular 6-monthly reminders ahead of renewal payments (including the opportunity to end the subscription)[footnote 62]

14-day cooling off periods, allowing the consumer to cancel the subscription without penalty or charge within that period, both at the start of the contract and when it renews[footnote 63]

a right for consumers to cancel a subscription contract without penalty or charge where the trader breaches certain key requirements applying to subscription contracts[footnote 64]

The outline above is not exhaustive. Businesses offering subscription services should therefore review the new obligations in detail and adjust their practices as necessary to ensure they comply, seeking legal advice if necessary.

Ensuring that services are performed with reasonable care and skill

Businesses must ensure that their services are provided with reasonable care and skill.

Consumer protection law requires that businesses use reasonable care and skill in providing services to consumers.[footnote 65]

Consumers purchase unregulated legal services to address very specific and often sensitive needs. In many cases, these will be one-off purchases. Consumers are unlikely to have wide experience of the services in question, and may be at a disadvantage relative to providers of those services in detecting shortfalls in quality. For many consumers, an unregulated legal service provider will be an alternative to more traditional vendors, such as solicitors’ firms. The requirement to use reasonable care and skill applies in that context.

Areas of particular relevance here include:

Competence

The service must be delivered by individuals possessing a degree of professional knowledge appropriate to the complexity of the service offered.

Suitability

Businesses should ensure that their services meet the legal requirements of the jurisdiction they are marketed for use in.[footnote 66] Similarly, businesses should ensure that they do not carry on ‘reserved’ legal activities unless they are legally permitted to do so.[footnote 67]

Selling additional services

Businesses should not use their position as adviser to ‘up-sell’ unnecessary or unsuitable services.

Clear advice

Unregulated providers of legal services must be clear about the nature and limits of the service they are providing. Simply including disclaimer language in contractual materials does not mean that an unregulated provider is absolved of this responsibility. Consumers should be informed when issues arise that impact the effectiveness of the service being delivered and that require other professional help to resolve (for example, tax issues).

Safeguarding of consumer assets

If the service involves long-term responsibility for consumer assets (for example, will storage) there will need to be safeguards to address not only ‘business as usual’ risks, but also to ensure that consumers do not suffer losses where the business itself changes, ceases or becomes insolvent.

Record keeping

Businesses should keep (and share with consumers, if appropriate), accurate records of the advice they are providing, and should ensure they comply with data protection law.[footnote 68]

Responsiveness and complaints handling

Businesses offering unregulated legal services should have processes for taking care of consumers’ requests or complaints promptly and effectively: consumers should also be given, before purchase, the business’s contact details and its complaints handling policy.

Prompt and timely service

Businesses are required to deliver services at the time agreed or, if none is agreed, within a reasonable time.[footnote 69] Delays that arise for reasons genuinely beyond a business’s control should be communicated to consumers appropriately, and failing to offer consumers a termination right (along with a refund) in such a case is likely to be unfair.

Where a service is not performed with reasonable care and skill, the consumer will have the right to request that the business provide the service again,[footnote 70] and (in certain circumstances) the right to a refund.[footnote 71] In addition, the consumer may pursue other legal remedies, including a claim for damages.[footnote 72] Contract terms which exclude or limit these obligations and consumer rights are not binding on the consumer.[footnote 73]

Ensuring that sales practices are not aggressive, or otherwise contrary to statutory obligations

Businesses must not use sales practices that amount to harassment, coercion, or undue influence, and they must not take additional payments without consent.

Aggressive sales practices

Consumer protection law prohibits practices that harass, coerce or use undue influence that are likely to affect consumers’ decisions about products.[footnote 74]

This covers a variety of behaviours, including:

staying in a consumer’s home after being asked to leave, or staying for so long that they feel compelled to purchase the products the representative is selling[footnote 75]

using knowledge about a consumer’s affairs gained in, for example, drawing up a basic will, to aggressively ‘upsell’ other products

making misleading, exaggerated or frightening claims regarding, for example, inheritance tax liabilities, to pressurise a consumer who has purchased will writing services to order additional complex trust products which the consumer would not otherwise purchase
